shortDescription: The division Bench of Justice Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Justice Alok Aradhe has dismissed the appeals of Twinstar Technologies Limited against the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) judgment that set aside the approval of its resolution plan for Videocon Industries Limited (VIL…

children: The division Bench of Justice Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Justice Alok Aradhe has dismissed the appeals of Twinstar Technologies Limited against the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) judgment that set aside the approval of its resolution plan for Videocon Industries Limited (VIL) and twelve other Videocon group companies. That judgment had also sent the matter back to the Committee of Creditors (CoC).

In its judgement, the Court also rejected erstwhile promoter Venugopal Dhoot's plea to bring the Videocon group's foreign oil and gas assets into the insolvency process of VIL. It also set out the considerations that should guide the NCLAT when remanding an approved resolution plan to the CoC.

Twinstar's amended plan had a total financial outlay of Rs 2,962.02 crore. It was approved by 95.09 per cent of the CoC's voting share when voting concluded on December 11, 2020. Against admitted claims of Rs 64,838.63 crore, the plan entailed a haircut of 95.85 per cent. It provided for an upfront payment of Rs 200 crore to the financial creditors. They were also to receive non-convertible debentures (NCDs) with a face value of Rs 2,700 crore and a coupon of 6.65 per cent, redeemable in instalments up to the sixth year. Bank of Maharashtra, IFCI Ltd., SIDBI and ABG Shipyard Limited dissented.

The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Mumbai, approved the plan on June 8, 2021. However, it was directed that the dissenting financial creditors be paid their liquidation value in cash, upfront, before any payment to the assenting creditors. Bank of Maharashtra, IFCI and SIDBI appealed, and the NCLAT stayed the approval on July 19, 2021. The CoC then told the NCLAT that it wished to reconsider its approval in the larger public interest. It did so through SBI, on behalf of assenting creditors holding about 94.98 per cent of the voting share. On January 5, 2022, the NCLAT set aside the approval and remitted the matter to the CoC. The CoC resolved later that month to invite fresh expressions of interest. In February 2022, while issuing notice, the Supreme Court asked it not to proceed further.

Upholding the NCLAT's view, the Court held that the plan breached Section 30(2)(b) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC). It relied on the three-Judge Bench ruling in Jaypee Kensington Boulevard Apartments Welfare Association v. NBCC (India) Ltd., which held that payment to a dissenting financial creditor can only be a payment in terms of money. "A plan which leaves the dissenting financial creditors to be discharged, in substance, through debentures redeemable over a period of six years does not provide for "payment" within the meaning of Section 30(2)(b) of the Code," the Court said.

Twinstar had relied on Clause 3.5.7 of the plan, which stated that dissenting creditors would be paid strictly as per Section 30(2)(b). The Court rejected this. "A general stipulation of compliance with the law cannot be a substitute for a specific provision in the plan as to how, when and in what form the dissenting creditors will be paid," it said.

The plan was also found to violate Regulation 38(1)(b) of the CIRP Regulations because it did not give the dissenting financial creditors priority over the assenting ones. The NCLT's direction for upfront cash payment was held to be "in substance modification of the resolution plan". That was impermissible, since only the CoC can alter a plan, by the requisite voting share.

The Court held that the NCLAT's power to remit a plan flows by necessary implication from its appellate jurisdiction. Neither the NCLT nor the NCLAT can modify a plan, and rejecting one may push the corporate debtor into liquidation, which the Code treats as a last resort. Twinstar had argued in the alternative that any reconsideration be confined to its existing plan.

The Court declined, saying it is not for the Adjudicating Authority, the NCLAT or the Supreme Court to dictate to the CoC the commercial course it should adopt. It also noted that the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 has added a proviso to Section 31(2). This allows the Adjudicating Authority to give the CoC notice to rectify defects before rejecting a plan. The Court said the amendment confirms the legislative policy that a defective plan should be remitted to the CoC.

The Court also rejected the argument that the CoC became functus officio once it approved the plan. "The CoC is not an adjudicatory authority," it said. Relying on Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power and Steel Limited, it held that the CoC continues to exist until the plan is implemented or a liquidation order is passed. Since the approval never attained finality, the CoC was within its right to revisit its decision. The Court distinguished Ebix Singapore and Amtek Auto as cases about resolution applicants trying to walk out of approved plans. "The binding character of a plan approved by the CoC presupposes a plan that is compliant with the Code," it said.

The Court did side with Twinstar on one issue. It found that the NCLAT erred in holding that prior approval of the Competition Commission of India had not been obtained. The CCI's approval was dated December 8, 2020, before the CoC voting concluded on December 11, 2020.

The foreign oil and gas assets comprise participating interests in four concessions in Brazil and in the Nunukan block in Indonesia. They are held through VIL's subsidiaries, including its wholly owned subsidiary VOVL Limited. On these assets, the Court upheld the NCLAT's judgment of May 14, 2026. It held that a holding company does not own the assets of its subsidiary. It added that clause (b) of the Explanation to Section 18 of the IBC excludes the assets of any Indian or foreign subsidiary of the corporate debtor. "Therefore, even though VOVL, namely subsidiary of VIL, may have interest in Brazilian and Indonesian assets, the same do not become the assets of VIL," the Court said.

The Bench held that Dhoot was estopped by his own conduct. Among other things, it noted that he had himself asked SBI to shift the facilities sanctioned to VIL and VOVL to VOVL alone. His Section 12A proposal had also expressly kept the offshore assets out of the business plan. Rejecting the plea to lift the corporate veil, the Court said, "The corporate veil is lifted to prevent fraud or the evasion of a statute, whereas here the statute itself, by Explanation (b) to Section 18, excludes the assets of a subsidiary". It found the allegations of fraud and collusion against SBI, the Resolution Professional and the CoC "general and bereft of the particulars required in law".

The Court also declined to interfere with the transaction approved in the insolvency process of VOVL. Under that transaction, BPRL Ventures B.V., an indirect wholly owned subsidiary of Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited, acquired the Videocon group's quotas in the Brazilian joint venture by exercising its right of first refusal. VOVL's CoC had approved it by 99.96 per cent of the voting share. The VIL Vendors Association represents about 97 unpaid suppliers of VIL, mostly MSMEs. Its appeal was dismissed with liberty to pursue such remedies as may be available under law.

Before parting, the Court said it was placing "guardrails on the power of remand, such that it is only used in the most appropriate situations." Remand is to be exercised only to further the objectives of the IBC: keeping the corporate debtor a going concern, ensuring fair and reasonable recovery for all classes of creditors, and maximising asset value. "A remand that advances none of these objectives is not justified merely because the power to order it exists," the Court said. Remand must rest on a finding of legal non-compliance and must be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. The NCLAT may also use it to restore the allocation of roles where the NCLT has modified a plan instead of remitting it. Every remand order must carry a strict direction to adhere to the timelines under the Code and the regulations.

GAIL (India) Ltd. had intervened because its claim would be extinguished if the plan were approved. The Court said GAIL's claim shall be dealt with by the Resolution Professional in accordance with the Code. It directed the NCLAT to decide GAIL's pending appeal in light of the judgment. The Union of India had argued that the corporate debtor's interest in oil and gas blocks under production sharing contracts is only a right of exploration and extraction. The Court left the Union at liberty to raise this before the Resolution Professional and the Adjudicating Authority.

Senior Advocate Guru Krishna Kumar appeared for Twinstar Technologies. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta appeared for the CoC, and Additional Solicitor General N. Venkataraman appeared for Bank of Maharashtra and for BPRL. Senior Advocates K.K. Venugopal and Gopal Sankaranarayanan appeared for Venugopal Dhoot. Senior Advocate Maninder Singh appeared for the VIL Vendors Association, Senior Advocate Nakul Dewan for Pertamina, and Senior Advocate Niranjan Reddy for the Resolution Professional of VIL. Additional Solicitor General Vikramjit Banerjee represented the Union of India, and Advocate Shashank Garg appeared for GAIL.
